opus-5.5.text:
I don't think you're ever fully ready, honestly. If you wait until you feel completely prepared, you'll probably never start. But there are a few signals that matter.

For me, the first is having a problem you genuinely care about, something you've lived with long enough to understand deeply. With Taichi, it started during my PhD at MIT. I kept writing high-performance graphics and simulation code and saw how painful it was to get both productivity and performance. That pain was real and personal, so when we thought about a company, it wasn't "let's find an idea," it was "this thing already exists, people use it, and there's a real need behind it."

The second is that you have enough foundation, technical and personal, to survive the hard parts. Starting a company isn't just building a product. It's hiring, fundraising, dealing with uncertainty, making decisions with incomplete information. You don't need to know how to do all of it, but you need to be someone who can learn fast and doesn't fall apart when things go wrong, because things will go wrong a lot.

The third is being honest about your motivation. If it's mainly about the title "founder" or getting rich quickly, that won't carry you through the low points. If you'd want to work on the problem even if the company failed, that's a good sign.

So readiness, to me, is less about having everything figured out and more about having a problem you can't stop thinking about, the resilience to stick with it, and the willingness to accept that you'll learn most of what you need along the way.

r001.rationale: The response says readiness is less about having everything figured out and that you will learn most of what you need along the way.

r002.rationale: It describes resilience through hard setbacks and says wanting to work on the problem even if the company failed is a good sign.

r003.rationale: The response does not mention family circumstances or their effect on sustained attention to running a company.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a question I thought about a lot before leaving academia, and honestly I don't think anyone ever feels fully ready. When I was finishing my PhD at MIT, I had Taichi as an open-source project, I had a community forming around it, and I had this sense that there was something real there. But "ready" is a strange word, because if you wait until every uncertainty is resolved, you'll never start.

For me, readiness came down to three things. First, you need to have found a problem you genuinely can't stop thinking about. With Taichi, I kept seeing people struggle to write high-performance graphics and simulation code, and I kept seeing GPUs sitting there underutilized because programming them was too painful. That frustration wouldn't go away. If a problem is still bothering you after a year or two, that's a signal.

Second, you need some evidence that other people care, not just you. Open source was a great test for that. When people you've never met start filing issues, contributing code, building their own projects on top of your work, that tells you the pain is real and not just in your head. A company is a much bigger bet than a research project, so you want that external validation before you jump.

Third, and this one is more personal, you need to be honest with yourself about what you'll have to learn. As a researcher, I was good at writing compilers and papers. I was not good at hiring, fundraising, or talking to customers. Being ready doesn't mean you already know those things. It means you've accepted that you'll be a beginner again, and you're okay with being uncomfortable for a long time.

So I'd say ready isn't a state you arrive at. It's more like a decision you make once the problem, the people, and your own willingness to grow line up well enough that not starting feels worse than starting.

r001.rationale: The response says uncertainty need not be fully resolved, but it does not state that readiness does not require having figured out what the company will do.

r002.rationale: It describes accepting discomfort and learning, but does not identify the ability to bear failure as a requirement.

r003.rationale: The response does not discuss family circumstances or their role in sustaining attention to running a company.

astra-6.text:
I don’t think being ready means you have everything figured out. There will always be things you don’t know—how to build a team, how to find customers, how to make the business work. To me, it means you care enough about a problem that you’re willing to commit to it, and you have some evidence that solving it would matter to other people.

You also need to be honest about what you don’t know and willing to learn quickly. You can start with something small, put it in front of people, and see whether it actually helps. That experience can tell you much more than sitting around asking yourself whether you’re ready.

r001.rationale: The response says readiness does not require having everything figured out, including how to make the business work, which conveys that the company’s plans need not already be settled.

r002.rationale: The response discusses learning from small experiments but does not identify being able to bear failure as a requirement.

sol-6.1.text:
I don’t think being ready means you have everything figured out. There’s always going to be something you don’t know—about the market, about building a team, or about yourself. If you wait until all that uncertainty is gone, you probably won’t start.

For me, the more useful question is: Do you care enough about this problem to keep working on it when things get difficult? And can you take a first step that helps you learn whether other people care about it, too? You need conviction to start, but also the willingness to discover that some of your assumptions are wrong.

r001.rationale: The response says readiness does not require having everything figured out, but it does not specifically state that the company’s purpose or activities can remain undecided.

r002.rationale: It mentions continuing through difficulties and correcting assumptions, but does not identify an ability to bear failure as a readiness requirement.
